---
title: 'Behind the maps'
subtitle: 'The journey from a question to a published map.'
---

## A repeatable process, room to experiment

Every investigation has its own question and visual approach. A shared workflow keeps the data traceable and makes it easier to revisit a result.

```{=html}
<ol class="pipeline" aria-label="Map-making workflow" role="list">
  <li><strong>Sources</strong><span>Find &amp; assess</span></li>
  <li><strong>Python</strong><span>Prepare the data</span></li>
  <li><strong>PostGIS</strong><span>Connect &amp; analyse</span></li>
  <li><strong>R</strong><span>Draw the map</span></li>
  <li><strong>Quarto</strong><span>Publish the story</span></li>
</ol>
```

### 01 / Find and assess the data

Start with the question. Record the publisher, source URL, retrieval date, licence, coverage, and limitations. Retain original downloads outside Git when they are large or cannot be redistributed.

### 02 / Prepare with Python

Download, clean, validate, and transform inputs. Check coordinate reference systems, missing values, duplicates, and geographic coverage before drawing conclusions.

### 03 / Connect in PostGIS

Use one shared PostgreSQL/PostGIS database, with `raw`, `staging`, and `shared` schemas for reusable datasets and a separate schema such as `w2027_01` for a weekly analysis. Keep transformations in versioned SQL. Simple investigations can use files directly.

### 04 / Make the map in R

Use `sf` and `ggplot2` as a starting point, choosing other tools when the story benefits from them. Check projections, legends, colour accessibility, labels, and uncertainty. Export a web image and a LinkedIn version at 1200 × 1200 or 1200 × 1500 pixels.

### 05 / Publish with Quarto

Each weekly page combines the map, a short interpretation, provenance, expandable code, and links to source files and the LinkedIn post. GitHub Pages serves the rendered site; visitors do not need access to the database.

## Reproduce an investigation

Weekly folders contain `prepare.py`, `analysis.sql`, `map.R`, `metadata.yml`, and `index.qmd`. The page explains which steps were actually used, their order, and dependencies. Prepared figures are committed when their licences permit it, so the public site can build without database credentials.
